processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Menghai: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), sold loose or pressed, with no ripe-style piling.
harvest_season: As usual across Menghai, spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: As with other Menghai raw pu-erh, dark olive leaves with paler buds.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear gold when young, as with young raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Typical of raw pu-erh, olive-green leaves softening as they steep.
taste_profile: A clear wild mountain character with notable bitterness; beyond that, little is recorded about how it develops across steeps.

brewing.notes: Because of the bitterness, start with short steeps and lengthen them slowly.

vintage_note: Like other raw pu-erh, it is sold by harvest year, usually spring material pressed the same year, then drunk young or stored. It is a minor name, so most lots come from small makers and the year is only as good as the maker.
description:
Mannuo, also written Mannong, sits at the northern edge of Menghai County in Mengwang township, near the borders with Lancang and Simao. It is a quiet name now, which is the interesting part of its story.

Its old trees are made into raw pu-erh in the usual way, with sun-drying and no ripe-style piling.

The tea is described as having a clear wild mountain flavour and notable bitterness. Brew it short at first and see how the bitterness behaves before you add leaf or time.

Buy by the year and by the maker. Do not mix it up with Nannuo Mountain, whose name looks and sounds close but is a different and much better known place.
history:
Mannuo was once an important stop on the route from Menghai to Lancang and a significant tea-producing area. When other routes opened, its tea lost prominence.

That isolation is credited with sparing many high-quality old trees through the 1950s and 1960s, by the account of tea-trade writers. No exact dates are documented for the rise or the decline.
